newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia launches rubber pact, urges fair prices.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia launches rubber pact, urges fair prices.

text.p: Malaysia, the world's third largest rubber producer, launched a global rubber price pact on Tuesday and urged consumers, especially the world's five big tyre makers, to support prices.

"If there is no fair and remunerative price for rubber, then producers will be forced to cut back on production and rubber prices will spiral like nobody's business," Malaysian Primary Industries Minister Lim Keng Yaik told reporters.

Speaking at the launch of the International Natural Rubber Agreement 3 (INRA 3), Lim said tyre makers such as Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co, Michelin, Bridgestone Corp, Continental and Firestone were mainly responsible for poor prices now.
Asian rubber markets have been sluggish for six months due to weak demand from tyre makers and other users who were constantly seeking lower prices, regional traders said.
Lim said tyre manufacturers always managed to raise the price of their products, despite stiff competition, while rubber growers have been faring less well.
In Thailand, the world's largest rubber producer, standard rubber cost an average $1.20 a kg, around the same as in Malaysia, traders said.
Lim declined to say what he considered a reasonable price, saying this was "up to market forces".
He also dismissed the possibility of Malaysia teaming up with Thailand and Indonesia to form a rubber cartel.

"Our idea is not to threaten consumers, but they should know that our economies are undergoing structural changes and we're growing less dependent on rubber and turning to other lucrative crops," Lim said.
"The tyre makers think if we stop (producing), they can turn to Vietnam and other growing economies, but don't forget that those countries are getting wise too."
Lim said Malaysia, for instance, was only producing about a million tonnes of rubber a year when it had the capacity to turn out 1.3 million tonnes.
He said the new world rubber price pact was also designed to be more sensitive to market changes.
The INRA 3 is the world's only remaining global commodity agreement with a buffer stock that allows the industry to buy and sell rubber to stabilise prices.
Two cycles of the agreement -- INRA 1 and INRA 2 -- have been completed under the administration of the International Natural Rubber Organisation (INRO).
The third cycle effectively begins on Tuesday, with a week-long meeting that will name Malaysia's Ahmad Zubeir Noordin as the new executive director of INRO.

The U.N.-brokered agreement is valid for four years and the lower indicator price for the buffer stock manager to intervene has been raised to 157 Malaysian/Singaporean cents per kg, based on the currency of the two countries, from 150 cents previously.
